vignette:
Marcus

Marcus was twenty-six when three men cornered him outside the marina where he kept his sailboat. It was a Tuesday evening in late October, the light already gone from the sky, and he'd stayed late to secure the lines before a storm system moved through. They came from behind the maintenance shed-he heard footsteps, turned, and then there was the smell of them, the sound of his own breathing, a hand closing around his wrist. One of them had a knife. He remembered the blade catching the sodium light from the parking lot, remembered the cold shock of it against his ribs, the way his body had simply obeyed-wallet, phone, watch, all of it falling into their hands while his mind seemed to separate from what was happening, as if he were watching from somewhere outside himself. They left him there, bleeding slightly, shaking. A security guard found him twenty minutes later.

The physical injuries healed within weeks. The Coast Guard medical team cleared him for duty. But something had fractured in how his mind held the experience, and in the year and a half since, Marcus had come to understand that the event had not stored itself as a coherent narrative but rather as fragments that refused to cohere. He could access pieces of it-the smell, the pressure of the hand, the gleam of the blade-but when he tried to assemble them into a sequence, into a story he could tell, the pieces would not fit. They seemed to exist in isolation, each carrying its own charge of fear, none of them connecting to form a whole that his mind could process and release. The most troubling part was that he could not seem to put what had happened into words. When his girlfriend Sarah asked him to talk about it, he would open his mouth and find himself unable to translate the fragments into language. The words simply would not come. He knew, abstractly, that he'd been robbed, that he'd been threatened, that he'd been afraid-but when he tried to articulate the actual experience, to shape it into sentences, the gap between the internal chaos and language felt unbridgeable.

What unsettled him most was the peculiar quality of certain memories: sometimes he could recall elements of the attack with almost photographic clarity-the texture of the asphalt where he'd stood, the exact timbre of one man's voice-yet feel nothing. No fear, no anger, no sense that it had happened to him. It was as though he were recounting something that had occurred to a stranger, something he'd read about or heard secondhand. Other times, the opposite would occur: a surge of dread would rise in him without any clear memory attached to it, a pure sensation of threat that had no narrative anchor. Sarah had noticed the change in him. He'd become quieter, more withdrawn. At the Coast Guard station, his commanding officer had remarked that Marcus seemed distant, less engaged in the camaraderie that had once defined his presence there. He still performed his duties competently, but the warmth had gone out of it.

Now, at twenty-nine, Marcus found himself sitting in a therapist's office for the first time, trying to explain why he'd finally come in. He'd hoped that time would knit the fragments together, that his mind would eventually find a way to organize what had happened into something coherent and manageable. It hadn't. Instead, the disconnected pieces seemed to have taken on a life of their own, surfacing at odd moments, refusing integration, leaving him caught between the terror of the fragments and the eerie numbness of detached recall. What he wanted most was to be able to tell the story-to himself, to Sarah, to anyone-as a coherent whole. What frightened him was the possibility that his mind would never allow that to happen, that he would remain forever trapped in these scattered, wordless pieces of an event he could not seem to fully claim as his own.
